intro: A local kernel deep in a network depends on a wider span of the original input. Stride changes the spacing of those dependencies.
task: Trace theoretical receptive-field span and input-space jump after every layer.
requirements: The three inputs are equal-length integer vectors, length 1..8, entries 1..8. Start with field r=1 and jump j=1.
For each layer set r=r+(kernel-1)*dilation*j, then j=j*stride. Return {"field": vector, "jump": vector}. Compute spans on an unbounded one-dimensional input, without boundary padding.

Use finite real numeric values of magnitude at most 1e6, excluding boolean inputs. Each array axis has 1..64 entries and at most 65536 elements total unless a stricter bound is stated. Return NumPy arrays for array outputs, preserve caller inputs, and raise ValueError for invalid inputs.

examples.name: Two local layers
examples.output:
{'field': [3, 5], 'jump': [1, 1]}
(NumPy arrays shown as lists; rounded to 12 significant digits.)

examples.output:

(NumPy arrays shown as lists; rounded to 12 significant digits.)

hints.title: Follow the data
hints.body: The previous jump converts a kernel offset to input-space distance.

hints.title: Check the boundary
hints.body: Expand the field before applying the current layer’s stride.

explanation: Composing local dependencies produces a larger receptive field. Jump tracks the spacing between consecutive output centers, so early strides magnify the effect of later kernels.
This theoretical span may contain gaps from dilation. It says which input range could matter, not that every location contributes equally on every example.
